The check_max_stack_depth pass happens after the verifier's symbolic
execution
column2: and attempts to walk the call graph of the BPF program

column1: ensuring that the stack usage stays within bounds for all possible call
chains. There are two cases to consider: bpf_pseudo_func and
bpf_pseudo_call. In the former case
column2: the callback pointer is loaded into

column1: a register
column2: and is assumed that it is passed to some helper later which

column1: calls it (however there is no way to be sure)
conservative and accounts the stack usage anyway. For this particular
case
column2: asynchronous callbacks are skipped as they execute asynchronously

column1: when their corresponding event fires.
The case of bpf_pseudo_call is simpler and we know that the call is
definitely made
column2: hence the stack depth of the subprog is accounted for.

column1: However
column2: the current check still skips an asynchronous callback even if

column1: a bpf_pseudo_call was made for it. This is erroneous
accounting for the stack usage of the asynchronous callback
be used to breach the maximum stack depth limit.
Fix this by only skipping asynchronous callbacks when the instruction is
not a pseudo call to the subprog.
